claims.text: A multiscale model that separates electronic and lattice heat transport will reduce predictive error for HfNbTaTiZr from about 50% to about 20%.
The model is applicable over 50–1200 K.
Below 200 K, electronic and lattice thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr are approximately equal.
Above 300 K, lattice thermal conductivity dominates in HfNbTaTiZr.
Lattice dominance above 300 K is especially pronounced in specimens containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen has a total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m) above 300 K.
The validation specimens can be produced by powder metallurgy as a near-defect-free variant and a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen variant.
KKR-CPA provides a first-principles treatment of configurationally averaged electronic properties in disordered alloys.
KKR-CPA can be used here to calculate the electronic thermal-transport contribution of HfNbTaTiZr.
Anharmonic lattice-dynamics or molecular-dynamics methods can capture phonon dynamics beyond a Debye approximation.
An iterative electron–phonon coupling module can quantify and correct non-additive effects between electronic and lattice heat transport.

Chemical disorder and lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys produce fluctuations in atomic masses and interatomic force constants that enhance phonon scattering and reduce lattice thermal conductivity.
Oxygen-induced point defects scatter both electrons and phonons in HfNbTaTiZr.
Disorder scattering captured by KKR-CPA produces a temperature-insensitive electronic contribution below 200 K.
Advanced anharmonic lattice dynamics can account for temperature-dependent phonon dynamics and higher-order anharmonicity.
The proposed lattice calculation properly captures both Umklapp scattering and oxygen-defect scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Simple analytical treatments cannot fully represent the combined effects of atomic-size, mass, and force-constant fluctuations in random high-entropy alloys.
Existing Debye-based estimates for HfNbTaTiZr typically have about 50% error and conflate lattice and electronic contributions.
Substantially different microstructures or uncorrected non-additive electron–phonon coupling may limit model transferability.

The hypothesis is falsified if measured electronic and lattice contributions differ from predictions by more than about 20%, if the contributions are not approximately equal below 200 K, or if lattice dominance is absent above 300 K.
